claim: NBR1 associates with photodamaged chloroplasts independently of ATG7.
source: Here, we show that upon exposing Arabidopsis plants to intense light, NBR1 associates with photodamaged chloroplasts independently of ATG7, a core component of the canonical autophagy machinery.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy imaging showing mCherry-NBR1 associated with chloroplasts in both nbr1 and atg7 cotyledon mesophyll cells upon HL exposure (Figure 1E and F), and by immunogold labeling and western blot data (Figure 2).

claim: NBR1 coats both the surface and interior of chloroplasts after high light exposure.
source: NBR1 coats both the surface and interior of chloroplasts, which is then followed by direct engulfment of the organelles into the central vacuole via a microautophagy-type process.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing NBR1-GFP either coating the surface or localizing inside chloroplasts (Figure 1A), and by immunogold labeling showing NBR1 on the surface and inside chloroplasts (Figure 2E).

claim: Photodamaged chloroplasts decorated with NBR1 are engulfed into the central vacuole via a microautophagy-type process.
source: NBR1 coats both the surface and interior of chloroplasts, which is then followed by direct engulfment of the organelles into the central vacuole via a microautophagy-type process.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts associated with deep tonoplast invaginations and inside vacuoles (Figure 4A, B, C).

claim: The relocalization of NBR1 into chloroplasts does not require the chloroplast translocon complexes embedded in the envelope.
source: The relocalization of NBR1 into chloroplasts does not require the chloroplast translocon complexes embedded in the envelope but is instead greatly enhanced by removing the self-oligomerization mPB1 domain of NBR1.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-GFP localization in toc132-2 mutant (Figure 9A and B) and YFP-NBR1mPB1 internalization in tic40-4 mutant protoplasts (Figure 9C, D).

claim: Removing the self-oligomerization mPB1 domain of NBR1 greatly enhances NBR1 relocalization into chloroplasts.
source: The relocalization of NBR1 into chloroplasts does not require the chloroplast translocon complexes embedded in the envelope but is instead greatly enhanced by removing the self-oligomerization mPB1 domain of NBR1.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing YFP-NBR1mPB1 localized inside chloroplasts at a higher frequency than wild-type NBR1 (Figure 7B and C).

claim: The delivery of NBR1-decorated chloroplasts into vacuoles depends on the ubiquitin-binding UBA2 domain of NBR1.
source: The delivery of NBR1-decorated chloroplasts into vacuoles depends on the ubiquitin-binding UBA2 domain of NBR1 but is independent of the ubiquitin E3 ligases SP1 and PUB4, known to direct the ubiquitylation of chloroplast surface proteins.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing YFP-NBR1ΔUBA2 failed to associate with chloroplasts after HL exposure (Figure 7B and C).

claim: The delivery of NBR1-decorated chloroplasts into vacuoles is independent of the ubiquitin E3 ligases SP1 and PUB4.
source: The delivery of NBR1-decorated chloroplasts into vacuoles depends on the ubiquitin-binding UBA2 domain of NBR1 but is independent of the ubiquitin E3 ligases SP1 and PUB4, known to direct the ubiquitylation of chloroplast surface proteins.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-GFP localized to photodamaged chloroplasts in pub4-2 and sp1-2 single and double mutants (Figure 8).

claim: nbr1 mutants have altered levels of a subset of chloroplast proteins upon high light exposure.
source: Compared to wild-type plants, nbr1 mutants have altered levels of a subset of chloroplast proteins and display abnormal chloroplast density and sizes upon high light exposure.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing approximately 3% of chloroplast proteins showed significant increase or decrease in abundance after HL in nbr1 mutant (Figure 6A).

claim: nbr1 mutants display abnormal chloroplast density upon high light exposure.
source: Compared to wild-type plants, nbr1 mutants have altered levels of a subset of chloroplast proteins and display abnormal chloroplast density and sizes upon high light exposure.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing a 16% reduction in chloroplast density in nbr1 compared to 25% reduction in wild-type after HL (Figure 5A and B).

claim: nbr1 mutants display abnormal chloroplast sizes upon high light exposure.
source: Compared to wild-type plants, nbr1 mutants have altered levels of a subset of chloroplast proteins and display abnormal chloroplast density and sizes upon high light exposure.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing altered RECA-GFP and chlorophyll areas in nbr1 chloroplasts after HL treatment (Figure 5C and D).

claim: Photodamaged chloroplasts lose envelope integrity, allowing cytosolic ligases to reach the chloroplast interior to ubiquitylate thylakoid and stroma proteins.
source: We postulate that, as photodamaged chloroplasts lose envelope integrity, cytosolic ligases reach the chloroplast interior to ubiquitylate thylakoid and stroma proteins which are then recognized by NBR1 for autophagic clearance.
evidence: Supported by electron microscopy showing Type-3 chloroplasts with ruptured envelopes (Figure 2C), and by immunogold labeling showing NBR1 inside chloroplasts with disrupted envelopes (Figure 2E and F). The claim is presented as a postulate by the authors.

claim: NBR1 recognizes ubiquitylated thylakoid and stroma proteins for autophagic clearance.
source: We postulate that, as photodamaged chloroplasts lose envelope integrity, cytosolic ligases reach the chloroplast interior to ubiquitylate thylakoid and stroma proteins which are then recognized by NBR1 for autophagic clearance.
evidence: Supported by the requirement of the UBA2 ubiquitin-binding domain for NBR1 association with chloroplasts (Figure 7), and by immunogold labeling showing NBR1 on thylakoids and stroma (Figure 2E and F). The claim is presented as a postulate by the authors.

claim: NBR1 has a new function in the degradation of damaged chloroplasts by microautophagy.
source: This study uncovers a new function of NBR1 in the degradation of damaged chloroplasts by microautophagy.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-decorated chloroplasts being internalized into vacuoles through microautophagy (Figure 4), and by the independence of this process from ATG7 (Figure 1E, F and Figure 4B, C).

claim: Under low light conditions, NBR1 is typically found in cytosolic puncta within cotyledons that likely represent aggresome condensates.
source: Under LL, NBR1 was typically found in cytosolic puncta within cotyledons that likely represent aggresome condensates (Svenning et al., 2011; Jung et al., 2020) and did not colocalize with chloroplasts seen by chlorophyll autofluorescence (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging (Figure 1A) and by citations to previous studies characterizing NBR1 localization (Svenning et al., 2011; Jung et al., 2020).

claim: Under low light conditions, NBR1 does not colocalize with chloroplasts.
source: Under LL, NBR1 was typically found in cytosolic puncta within cotyledons that likely represent aggresome condensates (Svenning et al., 2011; Jung et al., 2020) and did not colocalize with chloroplasts seen by chlorophyll autofluorescence (Figure 1).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing no colocalization of NBR1-GFP with chlorophyll autofluorescence under LL conditions (Figure 1A).

claim: After exposing seedlings to high light and allowing them to recover under low light for 24 hr, 2% of the chloroplasts in HL-exposed mesophyll cells became heavily decorated with NBR1-GFP.
source: After exposing seedlings to HL and allowing them to recover under LL for 24 hr, 2% of the chloroplasts in HL-exposed mesophyll cells became heavily decorated with NBR1-GFP (Figure 1A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 1A and B.

claim: Some NBR1-GFP signal in hypocotyl cells is associated with stromules after high light exposure.
source: Some NBR1-GFP signal in hypocotyl cells was also associated with stromules (Figure 1A).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-GFP on stromules (Figure 1A).

claim: NBR1-GFP-decorated chloroplasts show a significant decrease in chlorophyll fluorescence intensity after high light exposure.
source: In cotyledons exposed to HL, chloroplasts not labeled by NBR1-GFP had chlorophyll intensity values similar to those of control chloroplasts kept under LL. In contrast, NBR1-GFP-decorated chloroplasts showed a significant decrease in chlorophyll fluorescence intensity (Figure 1C), consistent with chlorophyll breakdown after photodamage (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by quantification of chlorophyll mean intensity shown in Figure 1C, and consistent with previous findings on chlorophyll breakdown after photodamage (Nakamura et al., 2018).

claim: NBR1-GFP-decorated chloroplasts show a statistically significant increase in the chlorophyll fluorescence intensity ratio measured at 517 and 683 nm after high light exposure.
source: As an indicator of chloroplast photodamage, we quantified the chlorophyll fluorescence intensity ratio measured at 517 and 683 nm (Nakamura et al., 2018), and found a statistically significant increase in this ratio for NBR1-GFP-decorated chloroplasts after HL exposure (Figure 1D).
evidence: Supported by quantification shown in Figure 1D, using a method from Nakamura et al., 2018 as an indicator of chloroplast photodamage.

claim: The recruitment of ATG8 to chloroplasts after high light exposure depends on the canonical ATG machinery.
source: Previous studies showed that the recruitment of ATG8 to chloroplasts after HL exposure depends on the canonical ATG machinery (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2018.

claim: mCherry-NBR1 associates with chloroplasts in both nbr1 and atg7 cotyledon mesophyll cells upon high light exposure.
source: Upon HL exposure, we detected by confocal microscopy mCherry-NBR1 associated with chloroplasts in both nbr1 and atg7 cotyledon mesophyll cells (Figure 1E and F).
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 1E and F.

claim: In both nbr1 and atg7 genotypes, mCherry-NBR1 signal coats the chloroplast surface as well as its interior after high light exposure.
source: In both genotypes, the mCherry-NBR1 signal coated the chloroplast surface (open arrows in Figure 1E) as well as its interior (solid arrows in Figure 1E), indicating that ATG7, and by inference ATG8 lipidation, were not required for recruiting NBR1 to chloroplasts upon HL exposure.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy imaging shown in Figure 1E, with arrows indicating surface coating and interior localization.

claim: ATG7, and by inference ATG8 lipidation, are not required for recruiting NBR1 to chloroplasts upon high light exposure.
source: In both genotypes, the mCherry-NBR1 signal coated the chloroplast surface (open arrows in Figure 1E) as well as its interior (solid arrows in Figure 1E), indicating that ATG7, and by inference ATG8 lipidation, were not required for recruiting NBR1 to chloroplasts upon HL exposure.
evidence: Supported by confocal microscopy showing mCherry-NBR1 association with chloroplasts in atg7 mutant (Figure 1E and F), and by inference from the known role of ATG7 in ATG8 lipidation.

claim: Three morphologically distinct chloroplast types are found in wild-type, atg7, and nbr1 cotyledons after 24 hr exposure to high light, often in the same cell although with different frequencies.
source: Based on the degree of structural integrity, we found three morphologically distinct chloroplast types often in the same cell although with different frequencies.
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy analysis of high-pressure frozen/freeze-substituted cotyledons (Figure 2A-C) and quantification (Figure 2D).

claim: Type-1 chloroplasts have normal thylakoids and electron-dense stroma.
source: Type-1 chloroplasts had normal thylakoids and electron-dense stroma; Type-2 chloroplasts had dilated and lighter stroma with thylakoid membranes partially disorganized and often displaced to one side of the chloroplast; and Type-3 chloroplasts contained highly disorganized thylakoids, light stroma, and clear signs of chloroplast envelope rupture (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Type-2 chloroplasts have dilated and lighter stroma with thylakoid membranes partially disorganized and often displaced to one side of the chloroplast.
source: Type-1 chloroplasts had normal thylakoids and electron-dense stroma; Type-2 chloroplasts had dilated and lighter stroma with thylakoid membranes partially disorganized and often displaced to one side of the chloroplast; and Type-3 chloroplasts contained highly disorganized thylakoids, light stroma, and clear signs of chloroplast envelope rupture (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2A-C.

claim: Type-3 chloroplasts contain highly disorganized thylakoids, light stroma, and clear signs of chloroplast envelope rupture.
source: Type-1 chloroplasts had normal thylakoids and electron-dense stroma; Type-2 chloroplasts had dilated and lighter stroma with thylakoid membranes partially disorganized and often displaced to one side of the chloroplast; and Type-3 chloroplasts contained highly disorganized thylakoids, light stroma, and clear signs of chloroplast envelope rupture (Figure 2A–C).
evidence: Supported by transmission electron microscopy images shown in Figure 2A-C, with Figure 2C specifically showing ruptured envelopes.

claim: Type-3 chloroplasts are significantly more abundant in atg7 cotyledons compared to wild-type.
source: Type-3 chloroplasts were significantly more abundant in the atg7 cotyledons, whereas their frequency in nbr1 cotyledons was indistinguishable from that in wild-type cotyledons (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of chloroplast types shown in Figure 2D.

claim: The frequency of Type-3 chloroplasts in nbr1 cotyledons is indistinguishable from that in wild-type cotyledons.
source: Type-3 chloroplasts were significantly more abundant in the atg7 cotyledons, whereas their frequency in nbr1 cotyledons was indistinguishable from that in wild-type cotyledons (Figure 2D).
evidence: Supported by quantification of chloroplast types shown in Figure 2D.

claim: All chloroplasts in wild-type and atg7 seedlings exposed to high light show significantly higher NBR1 labeling than those seen in nbr1 cotyledons.
source: Whereas we did not detect labeling of NBR1 in the cytosol, all chloroplasts in wild-type and atg7 seedlings exposed to HL showed significantly higher labeling than those seen in the nbr1 cotyledons (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunogold labeling with anti-NBR1 antibodies and quantification shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: NBR1 is not detected in the cytosol by immunogold labeling.
source: Whereas we did not detect labeling of NBR1 in the cytosol, all chloroplasts in wild-type and atg7 seedlings exposed to HL showed significantly higher labeling than those seen in the nbr1 cotyledons (Figure 2E and F).
evidence: Supported by immunogold labeling results shown in Figure 2E and F.

claim: Endogenous NBR1 is detected on the surface and inside wild-type and atg7 chloroplasts after high light exposure.
source: Corroborating the NBR1-GFP and mCherry-NBR1 confocal imaging results, endogenous NBR1 was detected on the surface and inside wild-type and atg7 chloroplasts (Figure 2E).
evidence: Supported by immunogold labeling shown in Figure 2E.

claim: Type-3 chloroplasts show the heaviest internal NBR1 labeling, both on thylakoids and on the stroma.
source: Among the three types of chloroplasts, Type-3 chloroplasts, which were most abundant in atg7 cotyledons (Figure 2D), showed the heaviest internal labeling, both on thylakoids and on the stroma (Figure 2F).
evidence: Supported by immunogold labeling quantification shown in Figure 2F.

claim: NBR1 is barely detected in either the total extract or the chloroplast fraction from wild-type plants kept under low light.
source: NBR1 was barely detected in either the total extract or the chloroplast fraction from wild-type plants kept under LL (Figure 2G).
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: After high light exposure, NBR1 becomes much more abundant in the chloroplast fraction of wild-type plants.
source: However, after HL exposure, NBR1 became much more abundant in the chloroplast fraction.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: The association of NBR1 with chloroplasts under both low light and high light is apparent in atg7 seedlings.
source: The association of NBR1 with chloroplasts under both LL and HL was also apparent in atg7 seedlings (Figure 2G), further confirming that ATG7 is not required for recruiting NBR1 to photodamaged chloroplasts.
evidence: Supported by western blot analysis shown in Figure 2G.

claim: ATG8 coats photodamaged chloroplasts in Arabidopsis.
source: ATG8 was previously reported to coat photodamaged chloroplasts in Arabidopsis (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2018.

claim: NBR1 interacts with ATG8.
source: Since NBR1 interacts with ATG8, we tested whether NBR1 and ATG8 were recruited to the same chloroplast population.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge in the context of the study. The interaction is well-documented in the literature and is the basis for testing whether they are recruited to the same chloroplast population.

claim: Neither mCherry-NBR1 nor GFP-ATG8 associate with chloroplasts under low light conditions.
source: As expected, neither mCherry-NBR1 or GFP-ATG8 associated with chloroplasts under LL conditions.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 12 hr after high light exposure, approximately 4% of total mesophyll chloroplasts are decorated by mCherry-NBR1.
source: By 12 hr after HL exposure, approximately 4% and 5% of the total mesophyll chloroplasts were decorated by either mCherry-NBR1 or GFP-ATG8, respectively, but remarkably only 1% of chloroplasts were decorated with both (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 12 hr after high light exposure, approximately 5% of total mesophyll chloroplasts are decorated by GFP-ATG8.
source: By 12 hr after HL exposure, approximately 4% and 5% of the total mesophyll chloroplasts were decorated by either mCherry-NBR1 or GFP-ATG8, respectively, but remarkably only 1% of chloroplasts were decorated with both (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 12 hr after high light exposure, only 1% of chloroplasts are decorated with both mCherry-NBR1 and GFP-ATG8.
source: By 12 hr after HL exposure, approximately 4% and 5% of the total mesophyll chloroplasts were decorated by either mCherry-NBR1 or GFP-ATG8, respectively, but remarkably only 1% of chloroplasts were decorated with both (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 24 hr after high light exposure, approximately 7% of chloroplasts are labeled with GFP-ATG8.
source: A similar trend was observed 24 hr after HL exposure; approximately 7% of the chloroplasts were labeled with GFP-ATG8, 5.5% were labeled with mCherry-NBR1 but only 2% of the chloroplasts were associated with both (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 24 hr after high light exposure, 5.5% of chloroplasts are labeled with mCherry-NBR1.
source: A similar trend was observed 24 hr after HL exposure; approximately 7% of the chloroplasts were labeled with GFP-ATG8, 5.5% were labeled with mCherry-NBR1 but only 2% of the chloroplasts were associated with both (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: At 24 hr after high light exposure, only 2% of chloroplasts are associated with both GFP-ATG8 and mCherry-NBR1.
source: A similar trend was observed 24 hr after HL exposure; approximately 7% of the chloroplasts were labeled with GFP-ATG8, 5.5% were labeled with mCherry-NBR1 but only 2% of the chloroplasts were associated with both (Figure 3A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3A and B.

claim: NBR1 and ATG8 associate with unique populations of chloroplasts.
source: This dichotomy suggests that NBR1 and ATG8 associate with unique populations of chloroplasts, consistent with their distinct dependence on the ATG machinery for chloroplast recruitment.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing minimal overlap between mCherry-NBR1 and GFP-ATG8 on chloroplasts (Figure 3A and B), and by inference from their distinct dependence on ATG machinery.

claim: GFP-ATG8 fails to label photodamaged chloroplasts in atg7 cotyledons.
source: As previously reported (Nakamura et al., 2018), GFP-ATG8 failed to label photodamaged chloroplasts in atg7 cotyledons.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 3C and D, and by citation to Nakamura et al., 2018.

claim: There is a significant decrease in the proportion of chloroplasts decorated by GFP-ATG8A in the nbr1 mutant at 6 hr during recovery from high light exposure compared to wild type.
source: Compared to wild type, we detected a significant decrease in the proportion of chloroplasts decorated by GFP-ATG8A in the nbr1 mutant at 6 hr during recovery from HL exposure; however, by 24 hr, similar proportions of both wild type and nbr1 chloroplasts were coated by GFP-ATG8A (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: By 24 hr after high light exposure, similar proportions of both wild type and nbr1 chloroplasts are coated by GFP-ATG8A.
source: Compared to wild type, we detected a significant decrease in the proportion of chloroplasts decorated by GFP-ATG8A in the nbr1 mutant at 6 hr during recovery from HL exposure; however, by 24 hr, similar proportions of both wild type and nbr1 chloroplasts were coated by GFP-ATG8A (Figure 3C and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 3C and D.

claim: NBR1 and ATG8A are recruited to different populations of photodamaged chloroplasts.
source: Taken together, these results showed that NBR1 and ATG8A are recruited to different populations of photodamaged chloroplasts and that NBR1 is only partially required for the early association of GFP-ATG8A with these organelles.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing minimal overlap between NBR1 and ATG8 on chloroplasts (Figure 3A and B), and by the observation that nbr1 mutation only partially affects GFP-ATG8A association at early time points (Figure 3C and D).

claim: NBR1 is only partially required for the early association of GFP-ATG8A with photodamaged chloroplasts.
source: Taken together, these results showed that NBR1 and ATG8A are recruited to different populations of photodamaged chloroplasts and that NBR1 is only partially required for the early association of GFP-ATG8A with these organelles.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing a significant decrease in GFP-ATG8A association in nbr1 mutant at 6 hr but not at 24 hr (Figure 3C and D).

claim: ATG8-associated chloroplasts are delivered to vacuoles through a microautophagic process that relies on the canonical ATG machinery.
source: Previous studies have shown that ATG8-associated chloroplasts are delivered to vacuoles through a microautophagic process that relies on the canonical ATG machinery (Izumi et al., 2017; Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citations to Izumi et al., 2017 and Nakamura et al., 2018.

claim: mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts associate with deep tonoplast invaginations after high light exposure.
source: After HL exposure, mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts associated with deep tonoplast invaginations (Figure 4A), which led to their vacuolar internalization by microautophagy, in a process topologically analogous to that previously described for ATG8-decorated chloroplasts (Izumi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts surrounded by the tonoplast marker YFP-VAMP711 (Figure 4A).

claim: mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts undergo vacuolar internalization by microautophagy in a process topologically analogous to that previously described for ATG8-decorated chloroplasts.
source: After HL exposure, mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts associated with deep tonoplast invaginations (Figure 4A), which led to their vacuolar internalization by microautophagy, in a process topologically analogous to that previously described for ATG8-decorated chloroplasts (Izumi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing mCherry-NBR1-positive chloroplasts being internalized into vacuoles (Figure 4A), and by comparison to the process described by Izumi et al., 2017.

claim: NBR1-positive chloroplasts are detected inside vacuoles 24 hr after high light exposure.
source: Similarly, we were able to detect NBR1-positive chloroplasts inside vacuoles of the mCherry-NBR1 seedlings stained with the vacuolar dye BCECF (Scheuring et al., 2015) 24 hr after HL exposure (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of mCherry-NBR1 seedlings stained with BCECF shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: NBR1-decorated chloroplasts are detected inside vacuoles of atg7 seedlings after high light exposure.
source: Surprisingly, NBR1-decorated chloroplasts were also seen inside vacuoles of atg7 seedlings (Figure 4B and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 4B and C.

claim: NBR1 associates with chloroplasts targeted for vacuolar degradation through ATG7-independent microautophagy.
source: Collectively, these results are consistent with NBR1 associating with chloroplasts targeted for vacuolar degradation through ATG7-independent microautophagy.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-decorated chloroplasts inside vacuoles in atg7 mutant (Figure 4B and C), and by the observation that NBR1 associates with chloroplasts independently of ATG7 (Figure 1E and F).

claim: The higher number of NBR1-positive photodamaged chloroplasts in atg7 seedlings does not arise from a failure to deliver these chloroplasts to the vacuole.
source: In addition, the higher number of NBR1-positive photodamaged chloroplasts in atg7 seedlings (Figure 2) did not seem to arise from a failure to deliver these chloroplasts to the vacuole but more likely to the higher accumulation of photodamaged chloroplasts in the atg7 mutant.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-decorated chloroplasts inside vacuoles in atg7 mutant (Figure 4B and C), and by the higher frequency of Type-3 chloroplasts in atg7 (Figure 2D).

claim: The higher number of NBR1-positive photodamaged chloroplasts in atg7 seedlings is more likely due to the higher accumulation of photodamaged chloroplasts in the atg7 mutant.
source: In addition, the higher number of NBR1-positive photodamaged chloroplasts in atg7 seedlings (Figure 2) did not seem to arise from a failure to deliver these chloroplasts to the vacuole but more likely to the higher accumulation of photodamaged chloroplasts in the atg7 mutant.
evidence: Supported by the higher frequency of Type-3 chloroplasts in atg7 (Figure 2D), and by inference from the observation that NBR1-decorated chloroplasts can be delivered to vacuoles in atg7 (Figure 4B and C).

claim: atg5 and atg7 mutants show reduced loss of chloroplasts after high light exposure.
source: If NBR1 is critical for targeting photodamaged chloroplasts to the vacuole, we reasoned that nbr1 mutations would reduce the loss of chloroplasts after HL, as it has been shown for the atg5 and atg7 mutants (Izumi et al., 2017).
evidence: Supported by citation to Izumi et al., 2017.

claim: Under low light conditions, atg7 mutant seedlings have a higher density of chloroplasts compared to wild type.
source: We found that, under LL conditions atg7 but not nbr1 mutant seedlings had a higher density of chloroplasts compared to wild type (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Under low light conditions, nbr1 mutant seedlings do not have a higher density of chloroplasts compared to wild type.
source: We found that, under LL conditions atg7 but not nbr1 mutant seedlings had a higher density of chloroplasts compared to wild type (Figure 5A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: Twenty four hours after high light exposure, there is a reduction in chloroplast density in wild-type, atg7, and nbr1 genotypes.
source: Twenty four hours after HL, there was a reduction in chloroplast density in all three genotypes but the decrease was less pronounced in atg7 and nbr1 (17% and 16% reduction, respectively) compared to the wild-type control (25% reduction; Figure 5A and B), consistent with impaired turnover of chloroplasts in both atg7 and nbr1 mutants.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The decrease in chloroplast density after high light exposure is less pronounced in atg7 (17% reduction) and nbr1 (16% reduction) compared to wild-type control (25% reduction).
source: Twenty four hours after HL, there was a reduction in chloroplast density in all three genotypes but the decrease was less pronounced in atg7 and nbr1 (17% and 16% reduction, respectively) compared to the wild-type control (25% reduction; Figure 5A and B), consistent with impaired turnover of chloroplasts in both atg7 and nbr1 mutants.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and B.

claim: The reduced decrease in chloroplast density after high light exposure in atg7 and nbr1 mutants is consistent with impaired turnover of chloroplasts.
source: Twenty four hours after HL, there was a reduction in chloroplast density in all three genotypes but the decrease was less pronounced in atg7 and nbr1 (17% and 16% reduction, respectively) compared to the wild-type control (25% reduction; Figure 5A and B), consistent with impaired turnover of chloroplasts in both atg7 and nbr1 mutants.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification (Figure 5A and B), and by inference that reduced loss of chloroplasts indicates impaired turnover.

claim: There is a decrease in both RECA-GFP signal (stroma) and chlorophyll autofluorescence (thylakoids) area in individual chloroplasts 24 hr after high light exposure in wild-type, nbr1, and atg7 genotypes.
source: Overall, there was a decrease in both RECA-GFP and chlorophyll area of individual chloroplasts 24 hr after HL exposure in the three genotypes.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A, C, and D.

claim: nbr1 and wild type RECA-GFP-decorated chloroplasts are similar in size under low light.
source: However, whereas the nbr1 and wild type RECA-GFP-decorated chloroplasts were similar in size under LL, the decrease in RECA-GFP area upon HL treatment was slightly more abrupt in nbr1 (19% reduction) than in control cotyledons (14% reduction; Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: The decrease in RECA-GFP area upon high light treatment is slightly more abrupt in nbr1 (19% reduction) than in control cotyledons (14% reduction).
source: However, whereas the nbr1 and wild type RECA-GFP-decorated chloroplasts were similar in size under LL, the decrease in RECA-GFP area upon HL treatment was slightly more abrupt in nbr1 (19% reduction) than in control cotyledons (14% reduction; Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: RECA-GFP-decorated atg7 chloroplasts are smaller than those in control and nbr1 cotyledons under low light.
source: RECA-GFP-decorated atg7 chloroplasts were smaller than those in control and nbr1 cotyledons and showed a small (6%) reduction in area upon HL treatment (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: RECA-GFP-decorated atg7 chloroplasts show a small (6%) reduction in area upon high light treatment.
source: RECA-GFP-decorated atg7 chloroplasts were smaller than those in control and nbr1 cotyledons and showed a small (6%) reduction in area upon HL treatment (Figure 5A and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and C.

claim: Chlorophyll areas are smaller in nbr1 and atg7 chloroplasts compared to wild-type control even under low light conditions.
source: Chlorophyll areas were smaller in nbr1 and atg7 chloroplasts compared to the wild-type control even under LL conditions, and underwent an attenuated reduction after HL exposure (21% and 18% in nbr1 and atg7, respectively), compared to control chloroplasts (36% reduction; Figure 5A and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: Chlorophyll areas in nbr1 and atg7 chloroplasts undergo an attenuated reduction after high light exposure (21% and 18% respectively) compared to control chloroplasts (36% reduction).
source: Chlorophyll areas were smaller in nbr1 and atg7 chloroplasts compared to the wild-type control even under LL conditions, and underwent an attenuated reduction after HL exposure (21% and 18% in nbr1 and atg7, respectively), compared to control chloroplasts (36% reduction; Figure 5A and D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5A and D.

claim: Although both atg7 and nbr1 retain more chloroplasts than control plants after high light exposure, the remaining chloroplasts in the mutants are smaller, both in stroma and thylakoid areas.
source: These results demonstrate that although both atg7 and nbr1 retained more chloroplasts than control plants after HL exposure (Figure 4E), the remaining chloroplasts in the mutants were smaller, both in stroma and thylakoid areas.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification showing reduced chloroplast density loss (Figure 5B) and smaller chloroplast sizes (Figure 5C and D) in mutants.

claim: ATG7 and NBR1 are both important for chloroplast turnover but control different aspects of chloroplast remodeling/turnover after high light radiation.
source: These unique chloroplast dynamics in nbr1, atg7, and wild-type plants suggested that although ATG7 and NBR1 are both important for chloroplast turnover, they control different aspects of chloroplast remodeling/turnover after HL radiation.
evidence: Supported by the differential effects of nbr1 and atg7 mutations on chloroplast density, size, and chlorophyll content (Figure 5), and by inference from these distinct phenotypes.

claim: Mean chlorophyll fluorescence intensity in nbr1, atg7, and nbr1 atg7 mutants is weaker than wild type under low light conditions.
source: Compared to controls, mean chlorophyll fluorescence intensity in all three mutants was weaker than wild type under LL conditions.
evidence: Supported by multiphoton imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mean chlorophyll fluorescence intensity decreases approximately 27-28% in wild type and atg7 mutant after high light exposure.
source: This intensity decreased approximately 27–28% in wild type and the atg7 mutant after HL (based on ratio of chlorophyll mean intensities between HL and LL values), but only 16% in the nbr1 mutant (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by multiphoton imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mean chlorophyll fluorescence intensity decreases only 16% in the nbr1 mutant after high light exposure.
source: This intensity decreased approximately 27–28% in wild type and the atg7 mutant after HL (based on ratio of chlorophyll mean intensities between HL and LL values), but only 16% in the nbr1 mutant (Figure 5E).
evidence: Supported by multiphoton imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mean chlorophyll intensity values from nbr1 atg7 double mutant under low light and after high light treatment are intermediate between those from the single nbr1 and atg7 mutant seedlings.
source: Unexpectedly, the mean chlorophyll intensity values from nbr1 atg7 mutant under LL and after HL treatment were intermediates between those from the single nbr1 and atg7 mutant seedlings.
evidence: Supported by multiphoton imaging and quantification shown in Figure 5E.

claim: Mutations in both NBR1 and ATG7 affect either chlorophyll abundance and/or chlorophyll photochemical properties even under low light conditions.
source: These results showed that mutations in both NBR1 and ATG7 affect either chlorophyll abundance and/or chlorophyll photochemical properties even under LL conditions.
evidence: Supported by multiphoton imaging showing altered chlorophyll mean intensities in mutants under LL conditions (Figure 5E), and by inference from these measurements.

claim: Over 1100 of the total proteins identified by MS/MS can be assigned to plastid-type compartments.
source: Based on Gene Otology (GO) term analysis, over 1100 of the total proteins identified by MS/MS could be assigned to plastid-type compartments, thus interrogating most, if not all, functions associated with this compartment.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and GO term analysis.

claim: Plastid proteins are well represented among those with decreased abundance upon high light exposure in wild type and mutants.
source: When analyzing this collection separately, we found that plastid proteins were well represented among those with decreased abundance upon HL exposure in wild type and the mutants (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), which was consistent with the overall reduction in chloroplast density and sizes seen in both backgrounds upon HL exposure (Figure 5).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and GO term analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), and consistent with confocal imaging data (Figure 5).

claim: In the three mutants, but not in wild type, proteins with increased abundance are found associated with plastids and organelles after high light exposure.
source: However, in the three mutants, but not in the wild type, proteins with increased abundance were also found associated with plastids and organelles (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D), consistent with impaired organelle turnover caused by the atg7 and nbr1 mutations.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and GO term analysis (Figure 6—figure supplement 1D).

claim: All four genotypes show an overall reduction in the abundance of some chloroplast proteins upon exposure to photodamaging radiation.
source: These results implied that whereas all four genotypes showed an overall reduction in the abundance of some chloroplast proteins upon exposure to photodamaging radiation, only the atg7, nbr1, and atg7 nbr1 mutants showed a significant accumulation of a subset of chloroplast proteins, which we hypothesized was caused by a lack of autophagic clearance.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing decreased abundance of chloroplast proteins in all genotypes (Figure 6A).

claim: Only the atg7, nbr1, and atg7 nbr1 mutants show a significant accumulation of a subset of chloroplast proteins upon exposure to photodamaging radiation.
source: These results implied that whereas all four genotypes showed an overall reduction in the abundance of some chloroplast proteins upon exposure to photodamaging radiation, only the atg7, nbr1, and atg7 nbr1 mutants showed a significant accumulation of a subset of chloroplast proteins, which we hypothesized was caused by a lack of autophagic clearance.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing increased abundance of chloroplast proteins in mutants (Figure 6A).

claim: The accumulation of a subset of chloroplast proteins in atg7, nbr1, and atg7 nbr1 mutants is hypothesized to be caused by a lack of autophagic clearance.
source: These results implied that whereas all four genotypes showed an overall reduction in the abundance of some chloroplast proteins upon exposure to photodamaging radiation, only the atg7, nbr1, and atg7 nbr1 mutants showed a significant accumulation of a subset of chloroplast proteins, which we hypothesized was caused by a lack of autophagic clearance.
evidence: This is stated as a hypothesis by the authors, based on the proteomics data (Figure 6A) and the known roles of ATG7 and NBR1 in autophagy.

claim: Wild-type plants show an overall decrease in chloroplast proteins after high light treatment (2.5% of total chloroplast proteins were less abundant and 1% were more abundant compared to low light conditions).
source: The wild-type plants showed an overall decrease in chloroplast proteins after HL treatment (2.5% of total chloroplast proteins were less abundant and 1% were more abundant compared to LL conditions) (Figure 6A).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the atg7 mutant, 9% of chloroplast proteins are more abundant after high light exposure and only 3.5% are less abundant.
source: For example, in the atg7 mutant, 9% were more abundant after HL exposure and only 3.5% were less abundant, while in nbr1 mutant, approximately the same number of chloroplast proteins (3% of the total chloroplast proteins) showed significant increase or decrease in abundance after HL.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: In the nbr1 mutant, approximately 3% of total chloroplast proteins show significant increase or decrease in abundance after high light exposure.
source: For example, in the atg7 mutant, 9% were more abundant after HL exposure and only 3.5% were less abundant, while in nbr1 mutant, approximately the same number of chloroplast proteins (3% of the total chloroplast proteins) showed significant increase or decrease in abundance after HL.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6A.

claim: The chloroplast proteins accumulating in the atg7 and nbr1 mutants localize to chloroplast envelopes, stroma, and thylakoids.
source: The chloroplast proteins accumulating in the mutants localized to chloroplast envelopes, stroma, and thylakoids (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that the atg7 and nbr1 mutations affects the homeostasis of all chloroplast subcompartments when plants are exposed to HL.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing proteins from different chloroplast subcompartments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2).

claim: The atg7 and nbr1 mutations affect the homeostasis of all chloroplast subcompartments when plants are exposed to high light.
source: The chloroplast proteins accumulating in the mutants localized to chloroplast envelopes, stroma, and thylakoids (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), indicating that the atg7 and nbr1 mutations affects the homeostasis of all chloroplast subcompartments when plants are exposed to HL.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing altered protein abundance in all chloroplast subcompartments (Figure 6—figure supplement 2), and by inference from this data.

claim: Both under low light and high light conditions, the three mutants (atg7, nbr1, nbr1 atg7) contain less chloroplast proteins compared to wild type.
source: Interestingly, when compared to the wild type, it became evident that both under LL and HL conditions, the three mutants contain less chloroplast proteins (Figure 6B), suggesting that chloroplast homeostasis is regulated by both ATG7 and NBR1, even under non-photodamaging conditions.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data shown in Figure 6B.

claim: Chloroplast homeostasis is regulated by both ATG7 and NBR1, even under non-photodamaging conditions.
source: Interestingly, when compared to the wild type, it became evident that both under LL and HL conditions, the three mutants contain less chloroplast proteins (Figure 6B), suggesting that chloroplast homeostasis is regulated by both ATG7 and NBR1, even under non-photodamaging conditions.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing lower chloroplast protein abundance in mutants under both LL and HL (Figure 6B), and by inference from this observation.

claim: 66% (25 of 38) of the chloroplast proteins significantly enriched in nbr1 are also more abundant in atg7.
source: We found that 66% (25 of 38) of the chloroplast proteins significantly enriched in nbr1 were also more abundant in atg7, whereas only 22% (25 of 115) of the more abundant chloroplast proteins in atg7 were also enriched in nbr1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Only 22% (25 of 115) of the more abundant chloroplast proteins in atg7 are also enriched in nbr1.
source: We found that 66% (25 of 38) of the chloroplast proteins significantly enriched in nbr1 were also more abundant in atg7, whereas only 22% (25 of 115) of the more abundant chloroplast proteins in atg7 were also enriched in nbr1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Of the 24 enriched proteins in the nbr1 atg7 double mutant, 16 proteins (67%) are shared with either atg7, nbr1, or both.
source: Of the 24 enriched proteins in the nbr1 atg7 double mutant, 16 proteins (67%) were shared with either atg7, nbr1, or both.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: For chloroplast proteins with decreased abundance upon high light exposure, the overlap between the single mutants is 38% (17 of 44 proteins) for atg7 and 46% (17 of 37 proteins) for nbr1.
source: For chloroplast proteins with decreased abundance upon HL exposure, the overlap between the single mutants was 38% (17 of 44 proteins) for atg7 and 46% (17 of 37 proteins) for nbr1 (Figure 6C).
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Of the 41 proteins decreasing in abundance in nbr1 atg7 plants, 21 proteins (51%) also show reduced abundance in one or both single mutants.
source: Of the 41 proteins decreasing in abundance in nbr1 atg7 plants, 21 proteins (51%) also showed reduced abundance in one or both single mutants.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data and Venn diagram analysis shown in Figure 6C.

claim: Both NBR1 and ATG7 control the degradation and overall homeostasis of chloroplasts after high light damage, but their functions are only partially overlapping.
source: These results suggest that both NBR1 and ATG7 controls the degradation and overall homeostasis of chloroplasts after HL damage, but their functions are only partially overlapping.
evidence: Supported by mass spectrometry proteomics data showing partial overlap in affected proteins between nbr1 and atg7 mutants (Figure 6C), and by inference from this data.

claim: The UBA2 domain of NBR1 is required for NBR1 to associate with chloroplasts after high light exposure.
source: Thus, these results suggest the UBA2 domain is required for NBR1 to associate with chloroplasts, whereas the PB1 domain negatively regulates NBR1 intra-chloroplast localization and/or promotes degradation of NBR1-filled chloroplasts.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing YFP-NBR1ΔUBA2 failed to associate with chloroplasts after HL exposure (Figure 7B and C).

claim: The PB1 domain negatively regulates NBR1 intra-chloroplast localization and/or promotes degradation of NBR1-filled chloroplasts.
source: Thus, these results suggest the UBA2 domain is required for NBR1 to associate with chloroplasts, whereas the PB1 domain negatively regulates NBR1 intra-chloroplast localization and/or promotes degradation of NBR1-filled chloroplasts.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing YFP-NBR1mPB1 localized inside chloroplasts at a higher frequency than wild-type NBR1 (Figure 7B and C). The claim includes alternative interpretations (localization vs. degradation).

claim: YFP-NBR1 mainly coats the chloroplast surface after high light exposure.
source: Thus, although the total percentages of chloroplasts labeled by YFP-NBR1 and YFP-NBR1mPB were similar (Figure 7C), YFP-NBR1 mainly coated the chloroplast surface whereas most of YFP-NBR1mPB was located to the chloroplast lumen.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Most of YFP-NBR1mPB is located to the chloroplast lumen after high light exposure.
source: Thus, although the total percentages of chloroplasts labeled by YFP-NBR1 and YFP-NBR1mPB were similar (Figure 7C), YFP-NBR1 mainly coated the chloroplast surface whereas most of YFP-NBR1mPB was located to the chloroplast lumen.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: YFP-NBR1mAIM is mostly detected as chloroplast coats after high light exposure.
source: Just like YFP-NBR1, YFP-NBR1mAIM was mostly detected as chloroplast coats (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: YFP-NBR1ΔUBA2 fails to associate with chloroplasts after high light exposure.
source: Interestingly, YFP-NBR1ΔUBA2 failed to associate with chloroplasts after HL exposure (Figure 7B and C).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 7B and C.

claim: Monomeric NBR1 proteins diffuse more easily through disrupted envelope membranes to reach the chloroplast stroma where they bind ubiquitylated chloroplast proteins.
source: We speculate that monomeric NBR1 proteins diffuses more easily through disrupted envelope membranes to reach the normally inaccessible chloroplast stroma where they bind ubiquitylated chloroplast proteins.
evidence: This is stated as speculation by the authors, based on the observation that NBR1mPB1 (which cannot oligomerize) is found more frequently inside chloroplasts (Figure 7B and C).

claim: The mPB1 domain of NBR1 is necessary for aggrephagy in plants as it mediates the formation of ubiquitylated cargo accretions.
source: The mPB1 domain of NBR1 is necessary for aggrephagy in plants as it mediates the formation of ubiquitylated cargo accretions (Svenning et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Svenning et al., 2011.

claim: NBR1-GFP localizes to photodamaged chloroplasts in pub4-2 and sp1-2 single and double mutants during recovery after high light exposure.
source: NBR1-GFP localized to photodamaged chloroplasts in pub4-2 and sp1-2 single and double mutants during recovery after HL (Figure 8), suggesting that at least these two E3 ligases are not critical for NBR1 association with photodamaged chloroplasts.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 8.

claim: At least the E3 ligases PUB4 and SP1 are not critical for NBR1 association with photodamaged chloroplasts.
source: NBR1-GFP localized to photodamaged chloroplasts in pub4-2 and sp1-2 single and double mutants during recovery after HL (Figure 8), suggesting that at least these two E3 ligases are not critical for NBR1 association with photodamaged chloroplasts.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1-GFP association with chloroplasts in pub4 and sp1 mutants (Figure 8), and by inference from this observation.

claim: The toc132-2 mutation does not affect the association of NBR1-GFP with chloroplasts or its localization into the chloroplast lumen after high light exposure.
source: The toc132-2 mutation did not affect the association of NBR1-GFP with chloroplasts or its localization into the chloroplast lumen (Figure 9A and B).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging shown in Figure 9A and B.

claim: YFP-NBR1mPB1 successfully internalizes into photodamaged chloroplasts in tic40-4 mutant protoplasts.
source: We found that YFP-NBR1mPB1 successfully internalized into photodamaged chloroplasts in tic40-4 mutant protoplasts.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging of transfected protoplasts shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: A larger proportion of chloroplasts with internal YFP-NBR1mPB1 signal is detected in tic40-4 compared to wild-type protoplasts after high light exposure.
source: In fact, we detected a larger proportion of chloroplasts with internal YFP-NBR1mPB1 signal in the tic40-4 compared to wild-type protoplasts (Figure 9. C, D).
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging and quantification shown in Figure 9C and D.

claim: The TIC-TOC complex is not required for the internalization of NBR1 into chloroplasts after high light exposure.
source: From this, we concluded that the TIC-TOC complex is not required for the internalization of NBR1 into chloroplasts after HL exposure.
evidence: Supported by confocal imaging showing NBR1 internalization in toc132-2 (Figure 9A and B) and tic40-4 (Figure 9C and D) mutants, and by inference from these observations.

claim: The rupture of the outer and inner envelopes in photodamaged chloroplasts allows for the diffusion of the ubiquitylation machinery and NBR1 from the cytosol into the chloroplast lumen.
source: We propose that the rupture of the outer and inner envelopes in photodamaged chloroplasts (Figure 2C) allows for the diffusion of the ubiquitylation machinery and NBR1 from the cytosol into the chloroplast lumen, promoting ubiquitylation of both stroma and thylakoid proteins and their subsequent binding to NBR1 for vacuolar degradation via microautophagy (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal by the authors, supported by electron microscopy showing envelope rupture (Figure 2C), immunogold labeling showing NBR1 inside chloroplasts (Figure 2E and F), and the requirement of UBA2 domain for NBR1 association (Figure 7).

claim: The diffusion of ubiquitylation machinery and NBR1 into the chloroplast lumen promotes ubiquitylation of both stroma and thylakoid proteins.
source: We propose that the rupture of the outer and inner envelopes in photodamaged chloroplasts (Figure 2C) allows for the diffusion of the ubiquitylation machinery and NBR1 from the cytosol into the chloroplast lumen, promoting ubiquitylation of both stroma and thylakoid proteins and their subsequent binding to NBR1 for vacuolar degradation via microautophagy (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal by the authors, supported by immunogold labeling showing NBR1 on stroma and thylakoids (Figure 2E and F), and by the requirement of UBA2 domain for NBR1 association (Figure 7).

claim: Ubiquitylated stroma and thylakoid proteins are subsequently bound by NBR1 for vacuolar degradation via microautophagy.
source: We propose that the rupture of the outer and inner envelopes in photodamaged chloroplasts (Figure 2C) allows for the diffusion of the ubiquitylation machinery and NBR1 from the cytosol into the chloroplast lumen, promoting ubiquitylation of both stroma and thylakoid proteins and their subsequent binding to NBR1 for vacuolar degradation via microautophagy (Figure 9E).
evidence: This is stated as a proposal by the authors, supported by the requirement of UBA2 domain for NBR1 association (Figure 7), and by confocal imaging showing NBR1-decorated chloroplasts being internalized into vacuoles (Figure 4).

claim: Autophagy in plants most commonly occurs through the formation of cargo-sequestering double-membrane-bound organelles called autophagosomes (macroautophagy) or through the direct engulfment of cargo by the vacuolar membrane (microautophagy).
source: In plants, autophagy most commonly occurs through the formation of cargo-sequestering double-membrane-bound organelles called autophagosomes (macroautophagy) or through the direct engulfment of cargo by the vacuolar membrane (microautophagy).
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about plant autophagy mechanisms.

claim: The molecular underpinnings of microautophagy are poorly understood.
source: Although the molecular underpinnings of microautophagy are poorly understood, the machinery behind macroautophagy involves more than 40 ATG (Autophagy Related) proteins whose actions are regulated by upstream phosphorylation events ultimately leading to formation of autophagosomes decorated with a conjugate of ATG8 bearing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (Xie et al., 2008).
evidence: This is stated as current knowledge in the field, contrasting the understanding of microautophagy with macroautophagy.

claim: The machinery behind macroautophagy involves more than 40 ATG proteins whose actions are regulated by upstream phosphorylation events ultimately leading to formation of autophagosomes decorated with ATG8-PE.
source: Although the molecular underpinnings of microautophagy are poorly understood, the machinery behind macroautophagy involves more than 40 ATG (Autophagy Related) proteins whose actions are regulated by upstream phosphorylation events ultimately leading to formation of autophagosomes decorated with a conjugate of ATG8 bearing phosphatidylethanolamine (PE) (Xie et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Xie et al., 2008.

claim: ATG8 lipidation is mediated by an enzymatic cascade sequentially involving the activating enzyme ATG7, the conjugating enzyme ATG3, and a ligase complex comprising an ATG5-ATG12 conjugate complexed with ATG16.
source: This lipidation is mediated by an enzymatic cascade sequentially involving the activating enzyme ATG7, the conjugating enzyme ATG3, and a ligase complex comprising an ATG5-ATG12 conjugate complexed with ATG16 (Ohsumi, 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Ohsumi, 2001.

claim: The ATG8-PE adduct is required for autophagosome assembly and for the selection of appropriate autophagic cargo through its interaction with autophagic receptors.
source: The resulting ATG8-PE adduct is not only required for autophagosomes assembly but also, through its interaction with a host of autophagic receptors, for the selection of appropriate autophagic cargo (Noda et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Noda et al., 2008.

claim: Metazoan SQSTM1/p62 and NBR1 promote the accretion of ubiquitylated proteins into larger condensates which are then encapsulated by autophagosomes for macroautophagic clearance (aggrephagy).
source: Among them, metazoan SQSTM1/p62 (Sequestosome 1) and NBR1 (NEIGHBOR OF BRCA1 gene 1) promote the accretion of ubiquitylated proteins into larger condensates which are then encapsulated by autophagosomes for macroautophagic clearance (aggrephagy; Bjørkøy et al., 2005; Komatsu et al., 2007; Nezis et al., 2008; Turco et al., 2021; Rasmussen et al., 2022).
evidence: Supported by citations to Bjørkøy et al., 2005; Komatsu et al., 2007; Nezis et al., 2008; Turco et al., 2021; Rasmussen et al., 2022.

claim: The PB1 domain present in both SQSTM1 and NBR1 mediates their mutual interaction and oligomerization into helical filaments.
source: The PB1 (Phox and Bem1 domain) domain present in both SQSTM1 and NBR1 mediate their mutual interaction and oligomerization into helical filaments (Ciuffa et al., 2015) which then promote the aggregation of ubiquitylated species (Jakobi et al., 2020; Turco et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Ciuffa et al., 2015; Jakobi et al., 2020; Turco et al., 2021.

claim: Mammalian SQSTM1 and NBR1 share a zinc-finger domain (ZZ) that can bind N-terminally arginylated proteins, polyubiquitylated proteins, and other cargo.
source: In addition, mammalian SQSTM1 and NBR1 share a zinc-finger domain (ZZ) that can bind N-terminally arginylated proteins, polyubiquitylated proteins, and other cargo (Cha-Molstad et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), a ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain with affinity for ubiquitin, and an ATG8-interacting motif (AIM) sequence that binds ATG8 (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Ichimura et al., 2008; Zientara-Rytter et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cha-Molstad et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021.

claim: Mammalian SQSTM1 and NBR1 share a ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain with affinity for ubiquitin.
source: In addition, mammalian SQSTM1 and NBR1 share a zinc-finger domain (ZZ) that can bind N-terminally arginylated proteins, polyubiquitylated proteins, and other cargo (Cha-Molstad et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), a ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain with affinity for ubiquitin, and an ATG8-interacting motif (AIM) sequence that binds ATG8 (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Ichimura et al., 2008; Zientara-Rytter et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seibenhener et al., 2004; Ichimura et al., 2008; Zientara-Rytter et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022a.

claim: Mammalian SQSTM1 and NBR1 share an ATG8-interacting motif (AIM) sequence that binds ATG8.
source: In addition, mammalian SQSTM1 and NBR1 share a zinc-finger domain (ZZ) that can bind N-terminally arginylated proteins, polyubiquitylated proteins, and other cargo (Cha-Molstad et al., 2015; Kwon et al., 2018; Wang et al., 2021), a ubiquitin-associated (UBA) domain with affinity for ubiquitin, and an ATG8-interacting motif (AIM) sequence that binds ATG8 (Seibenhener et al., 2004; Ichimura et al., 2008; Zientara-Rytter et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022a).
evidence: Supported by citations to Seibenhener et al., 2004; Ichimura et al., 2008; Zientara-Rytter et al., 2011; Sun et al., 2022a.

claim: NBR1, but not SQSTM1, contains a Four-Tryptophan (FW) domain, which at least in some fungal species helps recognize cargo for selective autophagy.
source: NBR1, but not SQSTM1, also contains a Four-Tryptophan (FW) domain, which at least in some fungal species helps recognize cargo for selective autophagy.
evidence: This is stated as established knowledge about the structural differences between NBR1 and SQSTM1.

claim: Plant NBR1 proteins uniquely harbor two UBA domains but only the C-terminal sequence (UBA2) binds ubiquitin.
source: The plant NBR1 proteins uniquely harbor two UBA domains but only the C-terminal sequence (UBA2) binds ubiquitin (Svenning et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Svenning et al., 2011.

claim: SQSTM1 and NBR1 can mediate selective autophagy of cargo in both ubiquitin and ubiquitin-independent manners.
source: Through these collective features, SQSTM1 and NBR1 can mediate selective autophagy of cargo in both ubiquitin and ubiquitin-independent manners.
evidence: This is stated as a conclusion based on the described features of SQSTM1 and NBR1, drawing from established knowledge.

claim: Most non-metazoan species encode only NBR1, whereas metazoans can express either or both SQTM1 and NBR1.
source: Most non-metazoan species encode only NBR1, whereas metazoans can express either or both SQTM1 and NBR1 (Svenning et al., 2011).
evidence: Supported by citation to Svenning et al., 2011.

claim: Arabidopsis NBR1 modulates tolerance to heat stress through recognition and sorting for degradation of proteotoxic ubiquitylated aggregates that accumulate at high temperatures.
source: For example, it modulates tolerance to heat stress through at least two mechanisms; recognition and sorting for degradation of proteotoxic ubiquitylated aggregates that accumulate at high temperatures (Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014), and the negative regulation of heat stress memory by mediating the clearance of heat-shock-related chaperones and their co-factors (Thirumalaikumar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014.

claim: Arabidopsis NBR1 modulates tolerance to heat stress through negative regulation of heat stress memory by mediating the clearance of heat-shock-related chaperones and their co-factors.
source: For example, it modulates tolerance to heat stress through at least two mechanisms; recognition and sorting for degradation of proteotoxic ubiquitylated aggregates that accumulate at high temperatures (Zhou et al., 2013; Zhou et al., 2014), and the negative regulation of heat stress memory by mediating the clearance of heat-shock-related chaperones and their co-factors (Thirumalaikumar et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Thirumalaikumar et al., 2021.

claim: Arabidopsis NBR1 targets the exocyst subunit EXO70E2 and its associated organelle EXPO for autophagic clearance.
source: Arabidopsis NBR1 also targets for autophagic clearance: (i) the exocyst subunit EXO70E2 and its associated organelle EXPO (Ji et al., 2020), (ii) misfolded protein aggregates (Jung et al., 2020), and (iii) viral capsid proteins (Hafrén et al., 2017) and pathogenic bacterial effectors (Dagdas et al., 2016; Dagdas et al., 2018; Üstün et al., 2018; Leong et al., 2022).
